# Shared fungal response: identification of commonly upregulated and downregulated genes

## 1. Initialization

Load the packages required for data manipulation, statistical modelling, and plotting.

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(broom)
library(purrr)
library(ggrepel)
```

**1) Removing genes with zero counts in every sample**

Remove genes that have no reads in any sample, since they do not provide information for the expression analysis.

First, convert the count values to integers and calculate the total number of counts for each gene across all samples.

```{r}
# Identify genes with zero counts
# Calculate total counts per gene
counts <- counts |>
  mutate(across(-gene_id, as.integer),
         total_counts = rowSums(across(-gene_id)))
```

Count how many genes have zero counts across all samples.

```{r}
# How many genes have zero counts?
counts |>
  filter(total_counts == 0) |>
  nrow()
```

Remove genes with zero total counts and discard the temporary column used for filtering.

```{r}
# Remove the rows with genes with 0 counts
# the remove the tmp total_count column previously created
counts_no0 <- counts |>
  filter(total_counts > 0) |>
  select(-total_counts)
```

Check the dimensions of the filtered dataset to see how many genes and sample columns remain.

```{r}
# Fast check
dim(counts_no0)
```

**2) Identify upregulated and downregulated genes**

3a. Normalising and transforming the counts

Convert raw counts into a normalised expression measure that can be used for exploratory analysis.

We use counts per million (CPM), followed by a log2 transformation. Adding 1 prevents taking the logarithm of zero.

```{r}
counts_log <- counts_no0 |>
  mutate(across(
      -gene_id,
      ~ log2((.x / sum(.x)) * 1000000 + 1) #log2tranformation of CPM
    )
  )
```

3b. Reshaping the expression table

Each sample is currently represented by a separate column. We reshape the table into long format, so that each row represents the expression of one gene in one sample.

```{r}
counts_long <- counts_log |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -gene_id,
    names_to = "sample_id",
    values_to = "expression"
  )
```

3c. Combining expression values with sample metadata

```{r}
expression_data <- counts_long |>
  left_join(metadata, by = "sample_id")
```

3d. Preparing the data for statistical modelling

We want to identify statistically significative genes whose expression changes following fungal stimulation compared with the control condition.

The control group is used as the reference category. This means that the estimated effect of each fungal stimulus represents its expression change relative to the control.

Donor is also included as a categorical variable to account for differences in baseline gene expression between individuals.

```{r}
expression_all_time_points <- expression_data |>
  mutate(
    stimulus = relevel(       # consider different fungi as experimental groups and RPMI as reference
      as.factor(stimulus),
      ref = "Control_group"
    ),
    donor = as.factor(donor)  # convert donors into discrete experimental grouping variable
  )
```

3e. Fitting linear models

We want to estimate the effect of each fungal stimulus on gene expression while accounting for donor-to-donor variation.

We fit a separate linear model for each gene at each time point.

The model includes:

- donor: accounts for differences in baseline expression between donors.

- stimulus: estimates the expression change associated with each fungal stimulus relative to the control.

The model assumes that the fungal stimulation effect is broadly consistent across donors.

```{r}
expression_all_nested <- expression_all_time_points |>
  group_by(gene_id, time) |>
  nest() |>
  mutate(
    model_object = map(
      data,
      ~ lm(
        formula = expression ~ donor + stimulus,
        data = .x
      )
    )
  )
```

Extract the coefficients and statistical results from each fitted model.

```{r}
expression_all_nested <- expression_all_nested |>
  mutate(
    model_results = map(model_object, tidy)
  )
```

And combine the results into a single table, retaining the gene identifier and time point.

```{r}
results_all <- expression_all_nested |>
  select(gene_id, time, model_results) |>
  unnest(model_results)
```

Retain only the coefficients associated with fungal stimulation. The donor coefficients are not needed for the subsequent analysis.

```{r}
results_all <- results_all |>
  filter(str_starts(term, "stimulus")) 
```

3f. Correcting for multiple testing

Since thousands of genes are tested, we adjust the p-values to account for multiple comparisons.

The Benjamini-Hochberg method is applied separately for each fungal stimulus and time point. The resulting adjusted p-values are stored in `q.value`.

```{r}
results_all <- results_all |>
  group_by(time, term) |>
  mutate(q.value = p.adjust(p.value, method = "BH")) |>
  ungroup()
```

3g. Identifying statistically significant genes

Identify genes with an adjusted p-value below 0.05.

```{r}
significant_all <- results_all |>
  mutate(is_significant = case_when(
    q.value < 0.05 ~ "Yes",
    q.value >= 0.05 ~ "No",
    TRUE ~ NA_character_
  ))
```

3h. Classifying gene regulation

We classify the direction and magnitude of the expression changes using the same effect-size thresholds as the reference study:

- Estimate greater than 0.9: upregulated.

- Estimate below -0.9: downregulated.

- Values between these thresholds: not strongly regulated.

We also simplify the stimulus names by removing the stimulus prefix.

```{r}
significant_all <- significant_all |>
  mutate(regulation = case_when(
    estimate > 1 ~ "upregulated",
    estimate < -1 ~ "downregulated",
    TRUE ~ "not strongly regulated")) |>
  rename(stimulus = term) |>
  mutate(stimulus = str_remove(stimulus, "stimulus"))
```

Retain only statistically significant genes.

```{r}
significant_all <- significant_all |>
  filter(is_significant == "Yes")
```

Keep only the columns needed for the subsequent analyses.

```{r}
significant_all <- significant_all |>
  select (gene_id, stimulus, time, regulation, estimate) 
```

## 4. Exploring the individual fungal responses

4a. Preparing the data for the scatter plot

We now want to investigate whether the baseline expression of a gene under control conditions is related to its estimated response to fungal stimulation.

First, we calculated the mean expression of each gene in the control samples, separately for each time point.

```{r}
control_means <- expression_data |>
  filter(stimulus == "Control_group") |>
  group_by(gene_id, time) |>
  summarise(
    control_expression = mean(expression)) |>
  ungroup()
```

Combine the control expression values with the estimated effects obtained from the linear models.

```{r}
scatter_data <- significant_all |>
  left_join(
    control_means,
    by = c("gene_id", "time")
  )
```

4b. Plotting baseline expression against estimated effect size

Each point represents one gene–fungus comparison at one time point. Is the gene's baseline expression level related to its response to fungal stimulation?

- X-axis: mean expression under control conditions.

- Y-axis: estimated expression change following fungal stimulation (control_expression: how much the gene is expressed under control conditions)

- Positive estimates indicate increased expression relative to control.

- Negative estimates indicate decreased expression relative to control.

```{r}
ggplot(
  scatter_data,
  aes(
    x = control_expression,
    y = estimate,
    color = stimulus
  )
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ time) +
  labs(
    title = "Control expression vs estimated effect size",
    x = "Mean control expression (log2 CPM)",
    y = "Estimated expression change",
    color = "Fungus"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Each dot represents one gene–fungus comparison at one time point

Points above zero indicate genes with higher estimated expression following fungal stimulation than under control conditions, while points below zero indicate genes with lower estimated expression following fungal stimulation than under control conditions.

This suggests that the transcriptional responses differ between fungal species.

- A point far right and high up: a gene that was already highly expressed in control and became even more expressed after fungal stimulation.

- A point far right and low down: a gene that was highly expressed in control but became less expressed after stimulation.

- A point far left and high up: a gene with low baseline expression that was strongly upregulated after stimulation.

4c. Comparing the distribution of effect sizes

We also want to compare the distribution of estimated expression changes between the three fungal stimuli at each time point.

The density curves show how the estimated effect sizes are distributed among statistically significant genes.

```{r}
ggplot(
  significant_all,
  aes(
    x = estimate,
    fill = stimulus,
    color = stimulus
  )
) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.25) +
  facet_wrap(~ time) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of effect sizes for regulated genes",
    x = "Estimated expression change",
    y = "Density",
    fill = "Fungus",
    color = "Fungus"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

4d. Comparing the proportions of upregulated and downregulated genes

We want to compare the relative contribution of each fungal stimulus to the number of significantly upregulated and downregulated genes.

First, count the distinct genes in each combination of time point, regulation direction and fungal stimulus. Genes classified as not strongly regulated are excluded.

```{r}
gene_counts <- significant_all |>
  filter(regulation != "not strongly regulated") |> 
  group_by(time, regulation, stimulus) |>
  summarise(
  n_genes = n_distinct(gene_id)) |>
  ungroup()
```

And now create a stacked proportional bar plot. Each bar represents 100%, allowing comparison of the relative contributions of the fungal stimuli.

```{r}
ggplot(gene_counts,
       aes(
         x = time,
         y = n_genes,
         fill = stimulus)) +
  geom_col(position = "fill", width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = n_genes),
    position = position_fill(vjust = 0.5),
    color = "black"
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ regulation) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of significantly regulated genes",
    x = "Time point",
    y = "Proportion of genes",
    fill = "Fungus"
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  theme_minimal()
```

4e. Comparing the number of upregulated and downregulated genes

Compare the absolute number of upregulated and downregulated genes induced by each fungus at 4h and 24h.

```{r}
gene_counts_individual <- significant_all |>
  filter(regulation != "not strongly regulated") |>
  group_by(time, stimulus, regulation) |>
  summarise(
    n_genes = n_distinct(gene_id)) |>
  ungroup()
```

Plot the gene counts separately for each time point and regulation direction.

```{r}
ggplot(
  gene_counts_individual,
  aes(
    x = stimulus,
    y = n_genes,
    fill = stimulus
  )
) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  facet_grid(time ~ regulation) +
  labs(
    title = "Differentially expressed genes following fungal stimulation",
    x = "Fungal stimulus",
    y = "Number of genes",
    fill = "Fungal stimulus"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```

4f. Comparing the effect sizes between fungi

Compare the magnitude and distribution of estimated expression changes for upregulated and downregulated genes across the three fungal stimuli.

```{r}
all_degs <- significant_all |>
  filter(regulation != "not strongly regulated")
ggplot(
  all_degs,
  aes(
    x = stimulus,
    y = estimate,
    fill = stimulus
  )
) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  facet_grid(time ~ regulation) +
  labs(
    title = "Individual fungal responses",
    subtitle = "Effect sizes of significantly regulated genes",
    x = "Fungal stimulus",
    y = "Estimated expression change",
    fill = "Fungal stimulus"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```

## 5. Identifying genes shared by all three fungi

We want to identify genes that are significantly regulated in the same direction by all three fungal stimuli at a given time point.

We retain only upregulated and downregulated genes, then group the results by gene, time point and regulation direction. A gene is considered shared when it appears in all three fungal conditions.

```{r}
shared_genes <- significant_all |>
  filter(regulation != "not strongly regulated") |>
  group_by(gene_id, time, regulation) |>
  filter(n_distinct(stimulus) == 3) |>
  ungroup()
```

Separate the shared genes into upregulated and downregulated groups.

```{r}
shared_up <- shared_genes |>
  filter(regulation == "upregulated")

shared_down <- shared_genes |>
  filter(regulation == "downregulated")
```

5a. Counting shared genes

Calculate the number of genes commonly upregulated or downregulated by all three fungi at each time point.

```{r}
shared_counts <- shared_genes |>
  group_by(time, regulation) |>
  summarise(
    n_genes = n_distinct(gene_id)) |>
  ungroup()
```

Visualise the number of shared upregulated and downregulated genes at 4h and 24h.

```{r}
ggplot(
  shared_counts,
  aes(
    x = time,
    y = n_genes,
    fill = regulation
  )
) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge", width = 0.65) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = n_genes),
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.65),
    vjust = -0.5
  ) +
  scale_x_discrete(limits = c("4h", "24h")) +
  labs(
    title = "Common transcriptional response to all three fungi",
    subtitle = "Genes regulated in the same direction by all fungi",
    x = "Time point",
    y = "Number of shared genes",
    fill = "Regulation"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

5b. Comparing shared genes between time points

Determine whether the genes commonly regulated by all three fungi at 4h are also commonly regulated at 24h.

First, extract the unique upregulated genes at each time point.

```{r}
up_4h_genes <- shared_up |>
  filter(time == "4h") |>
  distinct(gene_id)

up_24h_genes <- shared_up |>
  filter(time == "24h") |>
  distinct(gene_id)
```

Then we can use an inner join to identify genes present at both time points, and anti-joins to identify genes found at only one time point.

```{r}
common_up <- inner_join(
  up_4h_genes,
  up_24h_genes,
  by = "gene_id"
)

only_up_4h <- anti_join(
  up_4h_genes,
  up_24h_genes,
  by = "gene_id"
)

only_up_24h <- anti_join(
  up_24h_genes,
  up_4h_genes,
  by = "gene_id"
)
```

Repeat the same procedure for downregulated genes.

```{r}
down_4h_genes <- shared_down |>
  filter(time == "4h") |>
  distinct(gene_id)

down_24h_genes <- shared_down |>
  filter(time == "24h") |>
  distinct(gene_id)
```

Identify downregulated genes present at both time points or unique to one time point.

```{r}
common_down <- inner_join(
  down_4h_genes,
  down_24h_genes,
  by = "gene_id"
)

only_down_4h <- anti_join(
  down_4h_genes,
  down_24h_genes,
  by = "gene_id"
)

only_down_24h <- anti_join(
  down_24h_genes,
  down_4h_genes,
  by = "gene_id"
)
```

5c. Preparing the time-point overlap summary

Combine the results into one table showing how many genes are unique to 4h, unique to 24h, or shared between both time points.

```{r}
time_overlap <- bind_rows(
  only_up_4h |>
    summarise(n_genes = n()) |>
    mutate(regulation = "Upregulated", category = "4h only"),
  
  common_up |>
    summarise(n_genes = n()) |>
    mutate(regulation = "Upregulated", category = "Both time points"),
  
  only_up_24h |>
    summarise(n_genes = n()) |>
    mutate(regulation = "Upregulated", category = "24h only"),
  
  only_down_4h |>
    summarise(n_genes = n()) |>
    mutate(regulation = "Downregulated", category = "4h only"),
  
  common_down |>
    summarise(n_genes = n()) |>
    mutate(regulation = "Downregulated", category = "Both time points"),
  
  only_down_24h |>
    summarise(n_genes = n()) |>
    mutate(regulation = "Downregulated", category = "24h only")
)
```

5d. Visualising the overlap between time points

The plot compares the number of genes commonly regulated by all three fungi at each time point. It distinguishes genes found at only one time point from genes shared between both time points.

```{r}
ggplot(
  time_overlap,
  aes(
    x = category,
    y = n_genes,
    fill = category
  )
) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = n_genes),
    vjust = -0.5
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ regulation) +
  labs(
    title = "Shared fungal response across time points",
    x = "Time-point overlap",
    y = "Number of genes"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

## 6. Volcano plot of the shared genes

Visualise the estimated expression changes and adjusted p-values of genes commonly upregulated or downregulated by all three fungi.

We first retrieve the adjusted p-values from the original model results and combine them with the shared-gene information

```{r}
volcano_data <- shared_genes |>
  left_join(
    results_all |>
      rename(stimulus = term) |>
      mutate(stimulus = str_remove(stimulus, "stimulus")) |>
      select(gene_id, time, stimulus, p.value, q.value),
    by = c(
      "gene_id",
      "time",
      "stimulus"
    )
  )
```

Finally, we can create a volcano-style plot showing the estimated effect size on the X-axis and the negative logarithm of the adjusted p-value on the Y-axis.

Each point represents one shared gene in one fungal condition at one time point. Gene identifiers are displayed using labels, with `geom_text_repel()` helping to reduce label overlap.

```{r}
ggplot(
  volcano_data,
  aes(
    x = estimate,
    y = -log10(q.value),
    color = regulation,
    label = gene_id
  )
) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.7) +
  facet_grid(time ~ stimulus) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "upregulated" = "forestgreen",
      "downregulated" = "blue"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Volcano plot of the common transcriptional response",
    subtitle = "Genes significantly regulated in the same direction by all three fungi",
    x = "Estimated expression change",
    y = "-log10(adjusted p-value)",
    color = "Regulation"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## 7. Interpretation and comparison with the reference study

In our analysis, we identified genes commonly upregulated or downregulated by all three fungal stimuli at both 4h and 24h. However, no overlap was observed between the genes commonly regulated at the two time points. This suggests that the shared transcriptional response to fungal stimulation may be temporally dynamic, with distinct sets of genes contributing to the early and late responses.

The reference study identified differentially regulated transcripts using corrected *p*-values below 0.05 and a Log2FC greater than 0.9 for upregulated genes or below −0.9 for downregulated genes. It then examined the overlap between the responses to *A. fumigatus*, *C. albicans* and *R. oryzae* at 4h and 24h, as well as the temporal distribution of genes commonly regulated by all three fungi, which they defined as the “core” host response.

Unlike the reference study, our analysis did not identify a persistent core set of genes across both time points. This difference may reflect the distinct normalisation and statistical modelling approaches used in our analysis. We used CPM normalisation followed by log2 transformation and fitted gene-wise linear models accounting for donor and fungal stimulus. Although we applied the same corrected *p*-value and effect-size thresholds as the paper, the resulting gene lists were different.
